Solution: When fork is called, all the stack heap and other data variables of the process are copied into a new stack/memory space with a different pid number.

set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via

a trap?
student_answer:
There will be no trap in child process.
The process will be as follows:
1) syscall of fork form process parent (hardware changes parent to kernel mode)
2) does the fort, creates a child process (creates all entries needed for process)
3) calls sched_lock (before calling sched) (interrupt handler for parent process)
4) goes to scheduler (schedules the next process)

Now child is also a process in scheduling. We dont need to change its x process in userlevel by parent. Parents (level) need to be change which will be handled by the trap (syscall) given in question.

There is no need to return to child because it didn't even enter into kernel mode.

Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
rationale: The child process is indeed created in kernel mode and requires a context to execute there. The context is prepared to begin execution in a function and the kernel stack has the return address set to the return of the trap handler. This mimics a call and return from the handler, enabling the child process to leave the kernel mode and return to user space.

set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
student_answer:
When the child is forked, the current execution context and stackframe contents are all copied to the new PCB with a few exceptions. Everything is copied except PID, PPID, and the eax is set to 0 (which is equal to -1 for the parent).

So when the scheduler decides to go into the child process, it performs a context switch by loading its LIFO-program counter of the newly forked child.

Basically a new process is added to the ptable hence the scheduler and in READY state. Therefore the scheduler is invoked when yielded and it decides which process to run - also if it decides to run the child process it performs context switching from kernel (schedule) to child process by writing contents on its PCB.
reference_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

When fork() syscall is made, there is no trap in the child process, as it is made using the default trap handler. Now, syscall is trap handler. set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with

student_answer:
The trap/interrupt handler is not something specific to a process, but a property of the OS. So a child process also has the same trap/interrupt handlers as the parent process.
It returns from kernel mode to the user mode, and returns using the same return path as the parent called.
But if we're talking about how one child process returns from kernel mode (when invoked by a fork()), then it is a bit tricky, since the child process was just created and it doesn't make a system call on any other trap, so it's return path will also change.
reference_answer:

set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
rationale: You correctly identified that a child process has access to the same trap/interrupt handlers as the parent process. However, your explanation could be improved by emphasizing the significance of the child process starting execution at a function (e.g., forkret) and the setup of the kernel stack to return to the trap handler return address. c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
student_answer:
The child process points to the next instruction in the process which has to be run i.e. after fork() is called. Thus, whenever the child is scheduled, it will start its execution from that particular instruction. If it just needs a return value to emulate as if it actually entered from the trap handle of the child then we can easily determine to give the next function everything from the cpu.

The cpu doesn't care about it actually switching or not. It just cares about what value is there in the eip and as it should have the return value, which we have entailed as above. Thus, whenever the child process is scheduled, it will just return the user mode from any other signals to handle (live from an interrupt) , it will just restore everything the input function onwards as if it had actually returned from the function. The child never exits from trap. It just emulates as it did and keeps on executing the next instruction as if everything was done perfectly.
reference_answer:

Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function

set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

-> Trap handler identifies it as a syscall and hence go for executing a fork. syscall in kernel mode.
-> In kernel mode, a new process is allocated and copy the contents of the parent process. Trap frame is also copied from parent to child process.
-> Now, when sched is called, and if the child process is scheduled, we return from a syscall called _forkret_ and using the trapframe copied from above, child process can start executing from where parent has called fork.

the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

question:
c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
student_answer:
When fork() creates the child process, it is almost identical to the parent process, but there are few changes. The pid of the child process, for instance, is different (from the parent) and this is because fork() explicitly populates the childs Pcb with a different process identifier. The context is also copied from the parent to the child. In the parent, the context has a return address pointer to trapret (in the kernel code). In the child however, for k c changes the return address pointer in the childs context to foribret instead (forpat is also in the kernel code). Upon returning to foribret (which is flagged just before trapint in kernel.a), the return values of the registers are loaded to 0 and then execution flows to trapret. 
Thus, even though there was no trap in child process, as the parent's context is copied, the return address pointer from the child's context sends it to foribret which then reaches trapret which returns from trap.
reference_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
rationale: Nicely demonstrated! You explained the process accurately, from copying the parent's context to executing foribret instead of trapint. Your response effectively addresses the return path in the child process despite the absence of a trap.

In this copying, It also copies the trapframe of the parent process to the child process. So whenever, the child gets scheduled on the CPU, it reloads the trapframe of the parent and returns from kernel mode to the user mode via this registers.

Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
student_answer: When fork system call is made, a trapframe is explicitly created for child process. The new trapframe is exactly same as that of parent but with one difference that return value here is 0 opposed to pid in parent. Also, kernel stack is created to hold this trapframe. Now that trapframe exists, we can return to user mode like any other process does it.
reference_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from

student_answer: When a fork() call is made the os first allocates a process using allocproc() and then copies various attributes like, open-files, context, etc. from the parent to the child. It also allocates space for the user-stack of the new process. However since there was no trap for the child process, it copies the parents trap-frame to the child and sets the eax in the trapframe to 0. Now since the new process has almost everything set up as the parent process and the os has also set up the trapframe, the child process can return from the trap using trapget and since eax was set to 0 we also get the value returned by fork to be 0 in the child process.

set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via

a trap?
student_answer: In child process, there was no trap.
reference_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
rationale: A trap is not explicitly set for the child process. However, the context for the child process' execution is set up in a way that it appears as if a trap has occurred. This allows the child process to return to user mode.

the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
student_answer: When the fork() syscall is made, the parent creates a new process in the PCB by assigning memory, context, pid, etc in the kernel mode and once the child is created, the trap handler returns. Now a timer interrupt may occur. This interrupt makes the OS take control. Now the OS goes to the Ptable and decides on which process to run next. Now it may choose the child process and the user code in the child process starts running from the point after the fork() system thus timer interrupts that goes to the scheduler logic makes the child process run the user code.
reference_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

When fork call is made by parent, a new pcb and memory are created by the os for the child identical to the parent process.

c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
student_answer: When a fork() system call is made, it does two main things. First, it sets the return value to zero for the newly created child process. It also copies the trapframe of the process that created the child process to the newly created child's trapframe. Second, it makes the trapframe PC point to a special function called folk_det(). So, when a newly created child is scheduled for the first time, it first goes to folk_set() function. In this function, the child processes will return to the user mode from the kernel mode.
reference_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
rationale: The provided response correctly identifies some steps of the process but misses key details. PCB stores the information about trapframe also (address of the trapframe contents in the stack). - This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

question: Two      advantages of separating declaration from definition are: .....
student_answer:
1.) When declaration is separated from definition, then names of all the member functions inside a particular class can be found at the same place and it would make the body of the class look less cumbersome.
2.) When the functions are declared first and then defined later, then during defining a particular member function, we can use the other member functions of the class too inside this function's definition as they were already declared earlier and hence there will be no error. 
3.) Instead of writing a single long function, we can divide the function into two parts and then, use one of the function in the other function. For example, we can write a function to eject a drink from the vending machine, eject_drink(int drinkid) and also another function insert_coin(int value) which will take in the coin and find the drinkid corresponding to the inserted coin. c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
student_answer:
The kernel captures important information like the address of instruction to return to, as well as the return value, among other things, which are required to resume user process execution, in the trapframe.

The way fork behaves is that the child process's trapframe is copied from the parent's trapframe (with a definite change being in the return value of fork()).

Thus, the return-from-trap operation has the access to the information about which instruction address to continue from (eip). This is the same for parent and child, thus both return to the same instruction when scheduled by the scheduler.
reference_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
rationale: Your answer correctly identifies that the child process's trapframe is copied from the parent's, allowing both to return to the same instruction when scheduled. However, it doesn't delve into the context setup for the child to start executing in kernel mode. Including this detail would improve your explanation.

- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

student_answer: The context is switched to the parent; the point then calls wait(); and is given back to the child.
reference_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function

set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
rationale: The child process inherits the context of the parent process upon creation. It doesn't involve switching context to the parent process or calling wait(). The child process starts executing in kernel mode and uses a specific function (e.g., forkret) to return to user mode.

c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
student_answer:
* There was no trap in the child process, but the fork system calls set up the process / kernel stack in such a way that when the child process is scheduled, the kernel is as if it had earlier trapped into the kernel.
* In other words, the fork syscall fills up the kernel stack manually to make it look like it had trapped ie it fills up the stack with context / registers and other things that are to be popped from the stack during process trap. This is because the kernel has return address corresponding to the iret f and hence the first time the process is scheduled it returns from trap!
* For the return value, 0 is explicitly stored in eax and stored on stack which acts as the return value. 
* So, basically the return path for the child process is also through trap handles like the parent, the only difference being it was never actually trapped so we have to setup kernel during process creation such that it creates an illusion that the process was trapped to kernel mode.
reference_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

Here is how this works:
When the parent process calls fork, a new process is created which is almost an exact copy of the parent process. This includes copying the kernel stack data and the hence the trapframe is the state within state.
We accordingly set the return address from where the process must return and slap other registers such as eip - set accordingly.

- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

In the parent process, when fork() is called, it is syscall, hence an interrupt is generated. This leads process to go to trap handler, where corresponding to interrupt the corresponding IDT entry mapping is respected (hardware) and the syscall functionality is executed, leading to a child process.

set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)

and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.

c. When the fork() system call is made the child process is (almost) identical to the parent
process. In the parent process, the return path from kernel mode to user mode happens via
the trap/interrupt handler (system call is a trap/interrupt).
Explain the return path from the kernel mode to the user mode for the child process.
Specifically, there was no trap in the child process, so how does the child process return from
a trap?
student_answer:
When we fork a process in kernel mode we create a new process allocate pagetables open files, etc which are same as it's parent. Then we allocate a new page for kernel stack of new process and additionally copy trapframe of parent in trap frame of child. So we change eax value in new process and call trap which will pop all registers put in trapframe by alltraps. Then subsequently "iret" which will pop first register corresponding to user state in program like eip, cs, eflags, and change privilege mode and return to user process.

Code in x86:
np                       s2 + STACKSIZE - size_of(np->tf);   //np->new process
copy(p, &parent->np->tf);
np->tf.eax = 0;
trapret;    //pop all general purpose registers
iret;       //pop all user stack
reference_answer:
- When a child process is created and is ready to execute, it is in the kernel mode.
Child process needs context to execute in the kernel mode.
- The context for execution of the child is setup to start execution at the start of a function
(e.g., forkret) and the kernel stack of the child process is setup such that the return address is
set as the return of the trap handler (e.g., trapret)
- As a result, when a child process in the kernel is scheduled, it starts executing in a function
and returns from it to the return address (the trap handler return address).
- This emulates a call to the trap handler and a return from the handler and then proceeds with
the rest of the kernel stack unrolling to return to user space.
